title: Train-Validation-Test Split — 7 Learning Layers
subtitle: Topic: Dataset Partitioning and Model Evaluation · Subject: Data Preprocessing and Feature Engineering.
hero:
DATASET PARTITIONING · VISUAL ROADMAP

Train to learn. Validate to choose. Test to find out.

One dataset, three different jobs, and a final performance check on unseen records.

questions.stem: What is a Train-Validation-Test Split in Machine Learning, and why do we divide a dataset into three separate parts instead of using all available data to train a model?
options: The split trains three independent models on the entire dataset, then averages their results. It does not hold back examples, so all three models have already studied every record used for evaluation.

The split separates examples into Training, Validation, and Testing. Training teaches the model, validation helps choose settings, and untouched testing checks performance on new examples, rather than on data already used during development.

The split divides each example's feature columns into three sections. All rows train one model, while the separate groups of columns store input features, correct labels, and prediction results for comparison.

The split mainly reduces computer memory by processing examples in three batches. After learning from all batches, the model reports accuracy on those same examples rather than testing its ability to handle unseen data.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A Train-Validation-Test Split divides one dataset into three groups of examples. Training teaches the model, validation helps choose its settings, and testing checks the final model on untouched examples. Why not train on everything? The model may remember examples it has studied and look more accurate than it really is. Imagine a spam filter that performs well on familiar emails but misses new spam. Holding back test emails helps reveal that weakness.
questions.technicalExplanation: Training examples fit parameters; validation guides selection and tuning; testing independently estimates performance of the final selected procedure. Split design must respect independence, chronology and target deployment populations.

questions.stem: What is the specific purpose of the Training Set, Validation Set, and Test Set, and how does each dataset contribute differently to building, improving, and evaluating a Machine Learning model?
options: The Training Set chooses the final model by accuracy, validation provides examples for weight updates, and testing is repeatedly used for changing settings. This mixes development decisions with independent final evaluation.

Training data checks performance on unseen cases, validation runs the live model after deployment, and testing teaches the model weights during each training batch. This reverses the normal roles of the three datasets.

Training and validation both update weights during every batch, while testing determines hyperparameters and feature choices. The three group names describe storage locations rather than distinct responsibilities in model development.
The Training Set fits model weights, the Validation Set helps compare models and tune settings, and the Test Set evaluates the final chosen approach after development decisions are completed.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Each group has a specific job. The Training Set fits the model's weights and other parameters. The Validation Set helps compare versions, tune settings, and decide when to stop training. The Test Set measures the chosen model after those choices. Imagine predicting delivery times: past deliveries teach the model, separate deliveries help select its settings, and another untouched group checks how it handles new delivery records.
questions.technicalExplanation: Validation influences hyperparameters, thresholds, early stopping and architecture choices. A planned final refit on train+validation is possible before a single final holdout test if evaluation protocol permits.

questions.stem: Imagine having 10,000 labeled images of fruits and dividing them into 70% Training, 15% Validation, and 15% Testing. How many images belong to each group, and what would the model do with each group during the Machine Learning workflow?
options: Training has 7,000 fruit images, Validation has 1,500, and Testing has 1,500. The model learns from Training, tunes choices using Validation, and measures final recognition performance on the untouched Testing pictures.

Training has 7,000 fruit images, Validation has 2,000, and Testing has 1,000. The model learns from training examples, compares settings on validation examples, and measures final accuracy on the test examples.
Training has 7,000 images, Validation has 1,500, and Testing has 1,500. The model learns weights using all three groups, then reports accuracy on those same images as its final independent result.

Training has 7,000 images, Validation has 1,500, and Testing has 1,500. The model fits weights on Validation, uses Training to choose class labels, and adjusts hyperparameters after seeing Testing performance.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Multiply 10,000 by each percentage: 70% = 7,000 for training, 15% = 1,500 for validation, and 15% = 1,500 for testing. The model learns to recognize fruits from training pictures, uses validation to compare settings, and measures final recognition performance on untouched testing pictures. For example, it may learn apple and orange shapes during training, while validation identifies a better model version. The Test Set checks that version on different photographs.
questions.technicalExplanation: 10,000 × 70% = 7,000; 10,000 × 15% = 1,500. For two-stage splitting first set aside 15% test, then allocate 3/17 of the remaining 85% to validation.

questions.stem: How do we choose appropriate splitting ratios such as 70/15/15 or 80/10/10, and how do dataset size, class imbalance, stratified sampling, and random seeds influence the reliability of the split?
options: A 70/15/15 ratio is the best choice for every machine learning problem. Large datasets make class imbalance irrelevant, and different random seeds cannot affect whether the evaluation score is trustworthy.

An 80/10/10 ratio is always better because more examples train the model. Stratification means sorting labels alphabetically, while the random seed changes which class categories appear in the dataset.

The ratio depends on dataset size and enough examples for reliable evaluation. Stratification preserves approximate class proportions, and a fixed random seed makes a random split reproducible for later comparisons.

Split ratios depend mainly on the number of feature columns, not the number of records. Changing the random seed automatically prevents all time-series leakage and overlap between related customer records.
questions.explanation: Explanation: There is no single perfect ratio. Choose enough training examples to learn patterns and enough validation and test examples to measure performance reliably. Stratification helps keep similar class proportions in each random group. A fixed random seed makes the split repeatable, but does not make a poorly designed split safe. Imagine a factory dataset with rare machine failures: evaluation groups need enough failure cases to measure whether the model catches them.
questions.technicalExplanation: Stratified sampling approximately maintains target-label prevalence. Fixed random_state provides repeatability, not unbiasedness. Grouped and chronological data require different splitters.

questions.stem: How can we implement a Train-Validation-Test Split using Python and Scikit-learn, and why must preprocessing operations such as scaling, imputation, and feature selection be fitted only on the Training Set to prevent Data Leakage?
options: Call train_test_split twice, but fit scalers, imputers, and feature selectors on all examples before training. Using global statistics makes evaluation independent and prevents data leakage because every group is normalized identically.

Call train_test_split twice, then fit imputing, scaling, and feature selection using Training only. Apply the same learned transformations to Validation and Testing without fitting again, so evaluation information cannot leak into development.
Call train_test_split once, then fit_transform separately on Training and Testing. Each group learns its own preprocessing statistics, so the model can be evaluated without a separate Validation Set.

Call train_test_split twice but select features using labels from all three groups beforehand. Fitting the classifier only on training rows afterward ensures the earlier feature selection cannot leak information.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Use train_test_split twice: first hold out Testing, then separate Training and Validation. Fit scaling, missing-value filling, and feature selection only on Training. Reuse those learned rules to transform other groups. Otherwise, preprocessing can reveal information from the future evaluation data. For a house-price model, even using the mean house size from the Test Set to scale Training data creates leakage. A scikit-learn Pipeline helps keep the order correct.
questions.technicalExplanation: Fit all preprocessing within Training only. A Pipeline containing SimpleImputer, StandardScaler and SelectKBest should fit on training rows and be applied without fitting to Validation and Testing. Cross-validation must refit the whole pipeline inside each training fold.

questions.stem: Why can random splitting produce misleading evaluation results for time-series data, repeated customer records, or related samples, and how do chronological splitting, group-based splitting, and nested cross-validation help address these problems?
options: Random splitting is safe whenever a fixed seed makes the result repeatable. Chronological and group splits mainly sort file records, while nested cross-validation is only a faster way to shuffle examples.

Chronological splitting should train on the newest records and evaluate on the oldest records. Group-based splitting separates class labels, while nested cross-validation replaces tuning decisions with random sampling.

Random splits work for repeated customers whenever class percentages match across groups. Nested cross-validation automatically separates related customer records without any need to provide group identifiers or time constraints.

Random splits can mix future events or related customers across train and evaluation, inflating scores. Chronological splits preserve time, group splits keep linked records together, and nested cross-validation separates tuning from evaluation.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Random splitting is misleading when records are connected. With time-series data, it may let future information influence earlier predictions, so chronological splitting evaluates on later periods. Group-based splitting keeps one customer's records on one side. Nested cross-validation uses inner folds for tuning and outer folds for evaluation. Imagine forecasting electricity use: training on December observations before pretending to forecast October is unfair. Nested folds must also respect time and groups; nesting alone does not fix leakage.
questions.technicalExplanation: Chronological holdouts and TimeSeriesSplit preserve order; GroupKFold or StratifiedGroupKFold separate identities. Nested CV separates inner selection and outer performance estimation, but still needs suitable time/group-aware splitters.

questions.stem: How can repeated hyperparameter tuning on the Validation Set cause a model to indirectly overfit the validation data, and how should we design a reliable evaluation strategy involving cross-validation, a completely untouched Test Set, distribution shift checks, and final model selection?
options: Repeatedly tuning with validation scores can overfit decisions to that holdout. Use cross-validation during development, select a final model, check distribution shift, and evaluate once using a completely untouched Test Set.
Validation checks cannot overfit because validation examples never update model weights. Choose the best validation score, then tune on Testing to verify whether the settings can be improved further.

Combine Validation and Testing after every promising experiment to stabilize scores. Repeated adjustments using their combined score then produce the most independent estimate of performance on new examples.

Cross-validation removes every form of distribution shift, so testing is unnecessary. Select the model with the strongest training accuracy, then report accuracy on those training examples as the final evaluation.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Repeatedly choosing settings using Validation scores can overfit your decisions to that dataset, even if model weights never train on it. Use cross-validation to compare settings during development, then select a final approach and evaluate it on an untouched Test Set. Also check whether future data differs from training data. Imagine trying hundreds of advertising models: the highest validation score may be partly luck. Testing should be a fresh check, not another tuning opportunity.
questions.technicalExplanation: Repeated model selection on a fixed validation set introduces selection bias. Cross-validation or nested cross-validation assesses tuning more robustly, and a completely locked test estimates final generalization. Check distribution shift without using test outcomes to repeatedly redesign the model.
